draft.title: Economic growth and GDP
card: GDP
Gross domestic product is the value of all the goods and services made in a country in a year.
Economic growth
Economic growth is GDP rising over time. It is usually shown as a percentage change from one period to the next.
GDP counts what is made inside the country, whoever owns the business. It counts services such as haircuts and teaching as well as goods such as cars.
If GDP falls, the economy shrinks. If GDP rises, the economy grows.
draft.remember: GDP is the value of what a country produces in a year. Growth is GDP rising.

opts: A rise in the value of goods and services produced
A rise in the number of people in the country
A rise in the average price of goods and services
A rise in the number of businesses that open
a.why: Economic growth is GDP rising, which means more value of goods and services made. A rise in prices is inflation, which is a different idea.
a.clue: Growth is about GDP going up.

b.q: Last year a country's GDP was $900 billion. This year it is $936 billion. What has happened?
opts: The economy grew
The economy shrank
Prices rose in general
Unemployment fell
b.why: GDP rose from $900 billion to $936 billion, so the economy grew. The figures say nothing about prices or jobs, so those options cannot be shown from GDP alone.

a.best: A rise in the value of goods and services produced

problems.detail: The card defines growth as GDP rising in value, but does not say growth is measured in real GDP, adjusted for inflation. A rise in the dollar value of GDP can come partly or wholly from higher prices. Question b's dollar figures ($900b to $936b) could reflect inflation rather than more production, so 'the economy grew' is only safe if the figures are real GDP. Why (b) also says the figures 'say nothing about prices', which overlooks this. A short line such as 'measured after removing price rises (real GDP)', or labelling the figures as real GDP, would fix it.

check.summary: Both questions work as written. However, the card never says growth is measured in real (inflation-adjusted) GDP, so a rise in GDP's dollar value could be mistaken for growth when it is only higher prices. That affects question b's dollar figures and its why.
